personality_voice.book_baseline: In the book corpus for HBP, Sirius is already dead — he appears only through the memories, grief, and testimony of others. The corpus nevertheless constructs a clear personality baseline: he was restless, loyal, reckless, and emotionally intense. Harry recalls him 'prowling its dark musty rooms alone, imprisoned within the place he had wanted so desperately to leave' (Scene 28). Dumbledore describes the relationship with Harry as something Sirius valued deeply. Slughorn calls him 'a talented boy' who broke from Black family tradition by landing in Gryffindor (Scene 47). Snape's detention files record him alongside James Potter committing 'petty misdeeds' — hexing fellow students, accruing detentions — painting a portrait of someone mischievous, defiant, and disdainful of authority (Scenes 218-219). Harry attributes Sirius's death partly to Snape's taunts about cowardice, suggesting Sirius was proud, impulsive, and sensitive to challenges to his courage (Scenes 105-106). He is described as someone who 'hated those silver goblets' — careless of possessions — and who would not want Harry to 'shut himself away' (Scenes 133-140, 56). His personality is thus: brave to the point of recklessness, loyal, impulsive, emotionally intense, proud, bitterly unhappy in confinement, and darkly funny.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (HBP screenplay), Sirius Black does not appear, speak, act, or have his personality conveyed through any direct scene. He is referenced obliquely: Slughorn mentions 'Regulus Black. You no doubt know of his older brother Sirius. Died a few weeks ago. Talented boy.' (Film Scene 4). There is no scene, dialogue, flashback, or behavioral moment that conveys Sirius's personality, voice, humor, impulsiveness, restlessness, or emotional complexity.
personality_voice.difference: The film provides zero direct characterization of Sirius Black. The book corpus, while also dealing with Sirius posthumously, constructs a vivid portrait through Harry's grief, remembered behaviors, Snape's detention records, Slughorn's recollections, Dumbledore's eulogizing, and Harry's active resentment at Mundungus stealing Sirius's belongings. All of this personality texture is absent from the film corpus.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The score cannot be high when there is no film material conveying personality. The single film reference ('Talented boy') is a minor echo of Slughorn's book line and conveys nothing of Sirius's dominant traits, flaws, voice, or emotional texture. A score in the 10-13 range is appropriate: the name and a vague positive attribution ('talented') survive, but personality is substantially absent rather than actively distorted.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (book); Directly evidenced (film — absence of portrayal)

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books (HBP), Sirius's post-death narrative role is substantial even in absence. He functions as: (1) a catalyst for Harry's emotional state and motivation — Harry's grief and guilt over Sirius's death shape his entire arc in HBP; (2) a plot mechanism — his will bequeaths Harry Grimmauld Place and Kreacher, both of which become structurally important to Deathly Hallows; (3) a moral reference point — Harry measures his own courage and choices against what 'Sirius would have wanted' (Scene 56); (4) a source of conflict — the theft of his possessions by Mundungus triggers an active scene in Hogsmeade and a subsequent conversation with Dumbledore (Scenes 133-148); (5) a relationship anchor — his death drives Tonks's depression and changed Patronus (Scenes 65-67, 98-99, 187-193). These are all active narrative functions even for a dead character.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the film, Sirius functions solely as a name dropped in passing by Slughorn. The Grimmauld Place/Kreacher inheritance subplot is entirely absent. The Mundungus theft scene is absent. The Tonks grief subplot is absent or heavily reduced. Harry's emotional processing of Sirius's death — which in the book occupies multiple scenes and motivates his acceptance of danger — is not shown to derive from Sirius specifically. Sirius has no narrative agency and no structural function in the film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The book's entire Sirius-as-posthumous-agent structure — will, inheritance, Kreacher, Mundungus, Tonks, Harry's grief processing — is eliminated from the film. What remains is a one-sentence name-drop.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: This is a near-total elimination of narrative role. The character does not drive any scene, decision, relationship dynamic, or plot movement in the film. Score falls in the 6-9 range: role exists only as a name, agency is zero.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Sirius's posthumous motivations as constructed in HBP are: his desire to protect Harry (he left him everything), his need to act and prove himself despite confinement (retroactively established through Snape's taunts driving him to the Ministry), his bitterness at imprisonment and immobility, and his deep love for Harry as a surrogate son. These are expressed through Harry's retrospective understanding and Dumbledore's commentary (Scenes 52-57, 105-106).
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: No motivations are communicated in the film corpus. The single reference to Sirius conveys no internal state, no desire, no conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Complete absence. No motivation is shown, implied, or referenced beyond 'talented boy who died.'
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are absent rather than wrong, but absence here constitutes effective elimination. The score falls in the 5-7 range. It does not reach the lowest band because the book constructs motivations through grief and memory rather than direct scenes, and the film's omission is consistent with the overall compression — but it is still a substantial loss.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred from book corpus; Not enough evidence in film corpus

character_arc.book_baseline: Sirius's arc is complete before HBP begins — he died at the end of OotP. In HBP, his arc is retrospectively processed: Harry moves from raw grief and guilt (Scenes 28, 52-57, 63) through active anger (Mundungus theft, Scenes 133-140) to a kind of determined acceptance — 'Sirius wouldn't have wanted that, would he?' (Scene 56). The book uses Sirius's completed arc as a foundation for Harry's own arc. The arc as it exists in HBP is Harry's psychological integration of Sirius's death, which is a meaningful narrative function of the character even post-mortem.
character_arc.film_portrayal: No arc processing occurs in the film. Harry's grief over Sirius is not shown as a motivating force for his character in the HBP film, or if it is, it is not connected to Sirius by name or scene.
character_arc.difference: The retrospective arc — Harry's processing of Sirius's death as a through-line — is absent. This arc was already complete in terms of Sirius's own development, but its continued narrative function in HBP is eliminated.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Since the arc was completed before HBP begins, the flat arc in the film partially mirrors the flat (concluded) arc in the books. However, the book does meaningful work with Sirius's legacy in this volume that the film drops. Score sits in the 8-10 range: arc is incomplete in the film's handling of its aftermath, but the underlying arc (Sirius's own change) was already resolved, limiting the penalty.

key_relationships.book_baseline: In HBP, Sirius's key relationships as they register posthumously are: (1) Harry — godfather/surrogate son dynamic, Harry's grief is the most sustained emotional thread tied to Sirius in this book; (2) Kreacher — Sirius's mistreatment of Kreacher and Kreacher's betrayal is a direct cause of his death, and the inheritance of Kreacher by Harry is treated as morally complex; (3) Snape — lifelong mutual hatred, with Snape's taunts potentially having contributed to Sirius's death (Scenes 105-106); (4) Tonks — her grief and changed Patronus suggest deep feeling, possibly love (Scenes 65-67, 98-99, 187-193); (5) James Potter and the Marauders — referenced in Snape's detention files (Scenes 218-219) and Lupin's discussion (Scenes 156-160).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: None of these relationships are dramatized or even referenced meaningfully in the film corpus. Slughorn's passing mention conveys no relational dynamic. The Harry-Sirius relationship, which is the emotional core of HBP's opening, is not shown to animate Harry's behavior in the film.
key_relationships.difference: All key relationships are absent from the film corpus. The Harry-Sirius relationship — the most important — is not shown to be a source of Harry's grief, motivation, or character development in the film. The Kreacher subplot (which reveals Sirius's mistreatment and its consequences) is cut. The Snape-Sirius antagonism and its contribution to Sirius's death is not explored. Tonks's grief is either absent or not connected to Sirius.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: All key relationship dynamics are lost. Score falls in the 3-4 range: relationships are absent or functionally eliminated, not merely compressed.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book's Sirius is genuinely complex even in death: he was brave but reckless to the point of self-destruction; he loved Harry but his impulsiveness led directly to his own death; he was kind to Harry but cruel and dismissive to Kreacher, which had catastrophic consequences; he was trapped and miserable in Grimmauld Place, which made him unstable; he was idealized by Harry in ways the books gently complicate (Dumbledore's 'it was cruel you had such a short time' acknowledges the relationship's incompleteness). Snape's files show the pettier side of the Marauders. The Mundungus theft scene shows the indignity of Sirius's legacy being stolen. These are all nuances that construct a rounded, flawed, sympathetic but not sanitized figure.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: None of this complexity is present in the film. The single line 'Talented boy' is a simple positive attribution that sanitizes Sirius into a brief fond memory. The contradictions — recklessness, cruelty to Kreacher, impulsiveness, the bitterness of confinement — are entirely absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film presents Sirius as a name attached to a vague positive quality. All contradiction, flaw, relational complexity, and narrative texture is absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Complexity is almost entirely removed. The character is reduced to a proper noun and a two-word compliment. Score falls in the 5-7 range: not the absolute floor because the reference is not actively distorting, but it is functionally a blank where a complex character should be.

Cap 2 (80): Key relationships change substantially — applied
Cap 3 (75): Core book functions (will/inheritance, emotional anchor, Mundungus conflict) are absent rather than transferred — applied
Cap 4 (70): Film preserves only the character's name and a vague positive attribute, removing most defining characterization — applied
key_observations: Sirius Black in HBP is a dead character whose posthumous presence is nevertheless extensive and structurally important in the book: he drives the will/Kreacher/Grimmauld Place subplot, anchors Harry's grief and motivation, animates the Mundungus scene, shapes Tonks's emotional arc, and is invoked repeatedly as a moral reference point. In the film, he is reduced to a single passing reference by Slughorn — 'Died a few weeks ago. Talented boy.' — which conveys nothing of his personality, relationships, contradictions, or narrative function. The score of 41 reflects not active distortion but near-total absence: what little the film shows is not unfaithful in tone, but it is so minimal as to constitute an effective elimination of the character's book presence. Confidence is Medium rather than Low because the evidence of absence is clear and consistent throughout the film corpus.
